paragraphs: A poor man had twelve children and had to work night and day just to give them bread. When a thirteenth child was born, he was so distressed that he did not know what to do. He ran out onto the main road and decided to ask the first person he met to be the child’s godfather. The first to meet him was the good God, who already knew what troubled his heart. “Poor man, I pity you,” God said. “I will hold your child at his christening, take care of him, and make him happy on earth.” “Who are you?” the man asked. “I am God.” “Then I do not want you as a godfather,” the man said. “You give to the rich and leave the poor to go hungry.” He spoke this way because he did not know how wisely God divides wealth and poverty. So he turned away from the Lord and walked on. Then the Devil came to him and said, “What are you looking for? If you take me as your child’s godfather, I will give him plenty of gold and all the pleasures of the world.” “Who are you?” the man asked. “I am the Devil.” “Then I do not want you as a godfather,” the man said. “You deceive people and lead them astray.” He went on. Then Death strode up to him on withered legs and said, “Take me as godfather.” “Who are you?” the man asked. “I am Death, and I make everyone equal.” “You are the right one,” the man said. “You take the rich as well as the poor, without making any distinction. You shall be godfather.” Death answered, “I will make your child rich and famous, for anyone who has me as a friend can lack nothing.” “The christening is next Sunday,” the man said. “Be there on time.” Death came as promised and acted as godfather in the usual way.

When the boy had grown up, his godfather appeared one day and told him to come with him. He led him into a forest and showed him a herb growing there. “Now you shall receive your godfather’s present,” he said. “I will make you a famous physician. Whenever you are called to a patient, I will appear to you. If I stand at the sick person’s head, you may confidently say you will make them well again. Give them this herb, and they will recover. But if I stand at the patient’s feet, they belong to me. You must say that no treatment will work and no physician in the world can save them. But beware of using the herb against my wishes, or things may go badly for you.”

Before long, the young man was the most famous physician in the world. “He has only to look at a patient,” people said, “and he knows their condition at once, and whether they will recover or must die.” People came to him from far and wide and sent for him whenever someone was ill. They gave him so much money that he soon became rich. Then the King fell ill, and the physician was summoned to say whether he could recover. But when he reached the bed, Death stood at the sick man’s feet, and no herb grew that could save him. “If only I could cheat Death just once,” the physician thought. “He is sure to be angry if I do, but since I am his godson, he will turn a blind eye. I will risk it.” So he lifted the sick man and laid him the other way round, leaving Death standing at his head. Then he gave the King some of the herb, and the King recovered and became healthy again. But Death came to the physician, looking dark and angry. He shook a threatening finger at him and said, “You have tricked me. This time I will forgive you because you are my godson. But if you dare do it again, it will cost you your life. I will take you away with me myself.”

Soon afterwards, the King’s daughter became seriously ill. She was his only child, and he wept day and night until he began to lose his sight. He announced that whoever saved her from death would marry her and inherit the crown. When the physician came to the sick girl’s bed, he saw Death standing at her feet. He should have remembered his godfather’s warning. But he was so dazzled by the princess’s great beauty and the happiness of becoming her husband that he threw all caution away. He did not notice Death’s angry looks, or the hand raised to threaten him with its withered fist. He lifted the sick girl and placed her head where her feet had been. Then he gave her some of the herb. Instantly her cheeks flushed red, and life stirred in her again.

When Death saw that he had been cheated of his property for a second time, he strode up to the physician. “It is all over for you. Now your turn has come,” he said. He seized him so firmly with his ice-cold hand that he could not resist, and led him into a cave beneath the earth. There the physician saw thousands upon thousands of candles burning in countless rows. Some were tall, some half-sized, and some small. Every instant, some went out and others flared up, so that the flames seemed to leap here and there in constant change. “Look,” Death said. “These are the lights of human lives. The tall ones belong to children, the half-sized ones to married people in their prime, and the little ones to old people. But children and young people, too, often have only a tiny candle.” “Show me the light of my life,” the physician said, expecting it to be very tall still. Death pointed to a little stump just about to go out. “Look, there it is,” he said. “Oh, dear godfather,” the horrified physician said, “light a new one for me. Do it for love of me, so that I can enjoy my life, be King, and marry the King’s beautiful daughter.” “I cannot,” Death answered. “One must go out before a new one is lit.” “Then put the old one on top of a new one,” the physician pleaded, “so that the new one will start burning as soon as the old one is finished.” Death pretended he would grant the wish and took hold of a tall new candle. But he wanted revenge, so he deliberately made a mistake while fitting them together. The little stump fell and went out. At once the physician fell to the ground, and now he himself was in Death’s hands.
